videoIdeas.title: The 3 Second Rule That Kills Stage Fright
videoIdeas.hook: Your voice shakes for the first 10 seconds of any talk. Here's why — and how to kill it.
videoIdeas.rationale: Birdtart's practical, tactical 'here's exactly how to do X' videos (networking questions, cold emails) are pulling 900k+ views. You have zero tactical public-speaking how-tos in your top posts — it's a gap. Practical > abstract right now.
videoIdeas.script:
Your voice shakes for the first 10 seconds of any talk. That's not nerves. That's your body dumping adrenaline with nowhere to send it.

So give it somewhere. Before you speak, don't take a deep breath — everyone says that and it does nothing. Instead, press your feet flat into the floor and slow your first sentence down on purpose. Slower than feels natural.

Adrenaline wants speed. You give it control. By sentence three, it's gone.

The people who look calm on stage aren't calm. They just learned to spend the first 10 seconds buying themselves time instead of fighting their own body.

visuals.setting: Standing, mid-room, plain background. Smart-casual. Calm, grounded energy — you're demonstrating control, not hyping. Medium shot, steady frame.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'THE FIRST 10 SECONDS' appears as you stand dead still, then you deliberately slow down — a visible contrast between fidget and stillness.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-shake: film yourself visibly nervous for a beat, then cut to composed
On-screen punchline text: 'calm speakers aren't calm'
Pattern interrupt — start by saying 'take a deep breath' then shaking your head 'no, that's wrong'

videoIdeas.title: 5 Things Weak Leaders Always Do
videoIdeas.hook: Weak leaders all do the same 5 things. I've watched every one of them sink a team.
videoIdeas.rationale: The list format is dominating your niche right now — Daanish's '5 careers I don't want' hit 161k and '5 specialties' 30k. You have no list-format content. This packages leadership into a scannable, rewatchable format that the algorithm is rewarding.
videoIdeas.script:
Weak leaders all do the same 5 things. Watch for them.

One. They take credit in public and give blame in private. Strong leaders flip it.

Two. They avoid the hard conversation until it becomes a crisis. Then they act shocked.

Three. They confuse being liked with being respected. You can't lead people you're trying to impress.

Four. They hoard information. If your team only works when you're in the room, you're not a leader, you're a bottleneck.

Five. They never say 'I was wrong.' And everyone around them learns to do the same.

Leadership isn't the title. It's what you do when no one's clapping.

visuals.setting: Seated or standing, clean indoor setting, direct eye contact with camera. Confident, no-nonsense delivery. Count on fingers for each point.
visuals.visualHook: Big on-screen number counter '1...2...3...4...5' flashes up front so viewers know it's a list and stay for the full count.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on point 5 as a teaser, then 'but let's start at one'
On-screen text listing all 5 as fast cuts in the first 2 seconds
End-frame punchline text: 'which one are you?'

videoIdeas.title: Slowest Runner in the Race, Still in the Race
videoIdeas.hook: I finished near the back of my last race. I'd do it again tomorrow.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your single best post ('Might not be the fastest in the room. But I am in the room') hit 903 views — nearly double your next best. Personal + running + mindset is your proven format. Lean into what's already working for YOU, not just competitors.
videoIdeas.script:
I finished near the back of my last race. People faster than me had already showered and gone home.

And I'd do it again tomorrow.

Because here's what nobody tells you: the comparison game has no finish line. There's always someone faster, richer, further ahead. If that's your measuring stick, you lose every single day of your life.

The only honest question is — did you show up? Did you do the thing you were scared to start?

Most people never enter the race. They stand on the side critiquing the runners. Being slow and in the arena beats being fast in your imagination every time.

Might not be the fastest. But I'm in the room.

visuals.setting: Film mid-run or right after — outdoors, slightly out of breath, real sweat. Raw and unpolished beats studio here. Phone held or propped, natural light.
visuals.visualHook: Open on a wide shot of an empty finish line / you walking in last, on-screen text: 'everyone else went home.'
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-run, heavy breathing, no talking for 2 seconds
On-screen text punchline reveal at the end: 'but I'm in the room'
Pattern interrupt — start with 'I lost' then reframe

videoIdeas.title: How to Open Any Speech Without Saying 'Um, Hi'
videoIdeas.hook: Stop opening your talks with 'So, um, hi, my name is...' You've already lost the room.
videoIdeas.rationale: Birdtart's 'here are the exact questions/lines to use' format exploded (977k). People save tactical scripts they can copy. There's a clear gap — you own public speaking as a pillar but haven't given anyone a copy-paste opener.
videoIdeas.script:
Stop opening your talks with 'so, um, hi, my name is.' By the time you finish that sentence, the room's already on their phones.

The first line decides if they listen. So steal one of these.

Open with a question they can't answer easily: 'When was the last time you changed your mind about something that mattered?'

Or open with a hard number: 'Nine out of ten people in this room will never do the thing they're most capable of.'

Or just open mid-story: 'It was 2am and I was about to quit.'

Notice what's missing? Your name. Your title. Your thank-yous. Nobody came for that. Earn their attention first — then tell them who you are.

visuals.setting: Clean, well-lit, standing and addressing camera like it's an audience. Sharp, slightly fast energy. Smart clothing to match the 'speaking' topic.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text crosses out 'Hi, my name is...' with a red strike as you say it — instant visual 'don't do this.'
otherHookIdeas: Demonstrate the bad opener badly, then cut hard to the good one
On-screen text listing the 3 opener types as you say each
End with 'save this before your next talk' text prompt

videoIdeas.title: They're Not Debating You, They're Draining You
videoIdeas.hook: Some people don't want to win the argument. They want to waste your time. Here's how to tell.
videoIdeas.rationale: Saffanabanana's whiteboard/media-literacy explainers ('it takes a long time to brainwash you in a few seconds') are hitting 29-50k. Short, sharp 'here's how you're being manipulated' content is working in the niche. You can own this with a mindset/self-respect angle.
videoIdeas.script:
Some people aren't trying to win the argument. They're trying to drain you. And once you see it you can't unsee it.

Here's the tell. A real debate moves. New points, new angles, you both end up somewhere. A drain just loops. Same point, louder, recycled. They move the goalposts the second you make sense.

They don't want the truth. They want you tired.

Your energy is not infinite. Spending it on someone who's committed to misunderstanding you is a choice — and it's a bad one.

Walk away isn't weakness. Sometimes the strongest thing you'll do all week is refuse to keep playing a game you were never meant to win.

visuals.setting: Direct-to-camera, calm and controlled, indoor. Lower, steady tone — this is older-brother wisdom, not a rant. Tight framing on your face for intensity.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text: 'DEBATE vs DRAIN' split-screen style graphic appears in the first 2 seconds.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on the punchline 'they want you tired'
Hand-drawn / whiteboard-style loop diagram to echo what's working in the niche
On-screen text that loops/repeats to visually show 'the loop'

videoIdeas.title: The General Who Burned His Own Ships
videoIdeas.hook: In 711, a Muslim general landed in Spain and burned his own ships so his army couldn't retreat. There's a leadership lesson there you need.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your Tariq bin Ziyad / Andalusia post pulled 437 views — your second-strongest video and proof your audience responds to Islamic history with a modern lesson. Reframe the same era into a pure leadership pillar piece, tighter and with a clearer takeaway.
videoIdeas.script:
In 711, a Muslim general named Tariq bin Ziyad landed in Spain — and burned his own ships. His army looked back and saw the only way home going up in flames.

Then he told them: the enemy is ahead, the sea is behind, there is nowhere to go but forward.

That's not recklessness. That's leadership understanding something most people never do. People don't commit when they have an exit. The back door is where your resolve leaks out.

You do the same thing in your own life without noticing. The backup plan you keep 'just in case' is often the exact reason you never go all in on the first plan.

Sometimes leading — yourself or others — means closing the door behind you. No ships. No retreat. Just forward.

visuals.setting: Dim, slightly dramatic lighting, plain or textured background. Measured, storytelling cadence — slower, weightier than your tactical videos. Medium close-up.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text '711 AD' over a dark frame, then the single line 'he burned his own ships' — curiosity-driven cold open.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on 'there is nowhere to go but forward' then rewind to the start
On-screen text question: 'why would a general destroy his own escape?'
Hard cut from history to a modern frame of you: 'you do this too'

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your best post for a reason — 903 views, 114 likes, 11 comments. The caption 'Might not be the fastest in the room. But I am in the room' is your voice distilled: short, punchy, a reframe that makes people feel something and want to comment. Personal + running + mindset is clearly your winning lane.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: You're leaving the format on the table. This one line could BE a full video script, not just a caption. Build a repeatable 'lessons from running' series off this exact post — the audience already told you they want it. Also add one soft question to the caption ('what race are you avoiding?') to push comments past 11.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 437 views and strong retention topic — Islamic history with a hook date ('In 711 AD') pulls people in. This proves your audience will sit for a history-into-lesson story, and it diversifies you beyond running. Second-best video for a reason.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Zero comments despite 437 views means the story informed but didn't invite a response. The caption trails off mid-sentence ('wasn't built t…') — tighten it and end on a direct modern question or challenge. And land one clear leadership takeaway people can apply today, not just a history recap.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 'Never running through a park at night ever again 😭' — 374 views, 45 likes, strong like-to-view ratio (12%). This relatability/humour angle lands fast because it's human and low-effort to engage with. Proof your personality carries, not just your lessons.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: It's a dead end — pure relatable moment with no bridge to your pillars. These casual posts build warmth but won't grow the account alone. Use them as the hook, then pivot: a scary night run could open a mindset point about fear vs. actual danger. Convert the attention into a message.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Burnout is a sharp, relevant topic for young Muslims and the opener acknowledges a wide audience ('whether you're a medical student or not'). 209 views with genuine subject relevance — this is on-pillar for mindset.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: This reads like an app promo, and the numbers show it — 21 likes, 2 comments, your lowest engagement here. The caption shifts into product features ('identifying early signs, forecasting') and that kills it. Lead with YOUR take on burnout for 80% of the video, earn trust, then mention the tool at the very end. People engage with insight, not ads.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 289 likes — by far your most-liked post. The hadith framing ('Whoever sees an injustice…') gives it moral weight and your audience clearly rallies behind conviction and justice content. This tells you they respect you taking a clear stance.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: It's a Sidecar (carousel), not video, and has no view count and only 1 comment — likes without conversation or reach. The energy here belongs in a video where your delivery can carry the conviction. Also the caption cuts off ('not an option for…'); finish the thought with a direct call to the viewer, not just a statement, to turn 289 passive likes into real discussion.
